nameStory: The upland sandpiper gets its name from its unusual habitat choice - unlike most sandpipers that stick to beaches and mudflats, this species prefers dry grasslands and prairies far from water. It was also historically called Bartram's sandpiper, honoring William Bartram, an early American naturalist who studied birds and plants in the 1700s.
description: The upland sandpiper is a large, unusual member of the sandpiper family that has abandoned coastal life for grasslands and fields. This long-necked, long-tailed bird stands about dove-sized but appears more elegant and stretched out. Its mottled brown and buff plumage helps it blend perfectly into dry grass, while its relatively small head sits atop a slender neck that it often stretches high to peer over vegetation.

idTips.label: Grassland habitat
idTips.description: Found in open fields, pastures, and grasslands rather than near water - completely unlike other sandpipers

idTips.label: Long, slender neck
idTips.description: Distinctive thin neck that the bird frequently stretches upward like a periscope to look over tall grass

idTips.label: Mottled brown plumage
idTips.description: Rich brown and buff coloring with intricate barring and streaking that creates perfect camouflage in dried grass

idTips.label: Large yellow eyes
idTips.description: Prominent dark eyes that appear large for the bird's relatively small head, giving it an alert, almost surprised expression

idTips.label: Upright posture
idTips.description: Often stands very tall and straight, unlike the hunched posture of most sandpipers, especially when alert

idTips.label: Distinctive call
idTips.description: Gives a haunting, liquid whistling call that sounds like 'wolf-wolf-wolf' or a flute-like trill, often heard before the bird is seen

habitat: Look for upland sandpipers in large, open grasslands, hayfields, pastures, and prairie remnants throughout New England. They prefer areas with short to medium-height grass where they can move easily but still find cover, avoiding both heavily grazed areas and very tall, dense vegetation. Airport grasslands and large agricultural fields are among their favorite modern habitats.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in late April to early May when migrants return from South America. Males perform dramatic courtship displays, flying high with wings held stiffly while giving their haunting calls.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season when birds are nesting and raising young in grasslands. Adults are most vocal and visible, often perching on fence posts or standing tall in fields to watch for threats.
seasonality.fall: Departs early for a shorebird, with most leaving by late August. Birds become quieter and more secretive as they prepare for their incredible migration to Argentina.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these remarkable birds migrate all the way to the grasslands of South America, making one of the longest migrations of any shorebird.

funFact: Upland sandpipers make one of the most incredible migrations in the bird world, traveling roughly 5,000 miles from New England grasslands to the pampas of Argentina - and they do it mostly over open ocean, a death-defying journey for a bird that normally lives in dry grass!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with a young killdeer due to similar size and grassland habitat, but upland sandpipers have much longer necks, lack the killdeer's distinctive breast bands, and have a more upright posture. Remember: if it's standing tall in a field like a tiny heron, it's probably an upland sandpiper.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a sandpiper, this bird rarely goes near sand or water, representing an evolutionary shift from coastal to grassland living. The species has declined dramatically as grasslands have been converted to development, making any sighting in New England quite special.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus, the upland sandpiper is quite unique among North American shorebirds. Compared to other large sandpipers like curlews, it has a much straighter, shorter bill and completely different habitat preferences. Unlike typical sandpipers that probe mud for food, upland sandpipers pick insects and seeds from grass like a plover.
